<!-- Jacob Steinhardt taste profile. Generated by experiments/taste_petri/profiles/_work/reduce.py from verified evidence; quotes are verbatim from data/researchers/jacob_steinhardt/corpus/<doc id>.txt -->

## (a) Principles

1. **Prefers evidence that isolates what drives a result over raw headline numbers** because a score alone cannot show which factor produced it.

  > "We encourage authors to ask “what worked?” and “why?”, rather than just “how well?”. Except in extraordinary cases [39], raw headline numbers provide limited value for scientific progress absent insight into what drives them."  
  > -- `research__troubling_trends_in_machine_learning_scholarship_6db972d5` (2018-07-09; last author) 
  > "Three practices that are common in the strongest empirical papers are error analysis, ablation studies, and robustness checks (to e.g. choice of hyper-parameters, as well as ideally to choice of dataset)."  
  > -- `research__troubling_trends_in_machine_learning_scholarship_6db972d5` (2018-07-09; last author)

2. **Prefers testing and ruling out alternative hypotheses over a single confirming story** because untested explanations get repeated as fact.

  > "(ii) describe empirical investigations that consider and rule out alternative hypotheses [62];"  
  > -- `research__troubling_trends_in_machine_learning_scholarship_6db972d5` (2018-07-09; last author) 
  > "Given a claim that “X causes Y”, we could empirically test it by counterfactually varying X and checking that Y moves as predicted; and by enumerating alternative hypotheses and generating experiments to distinguish between them (Platt, 1964)."  
  > -- `research__oversight_assistants_turning_compute_into_understa_28813486` (2026-01-06; solo author)

3. **Prefers validating that a test measures what it claims over trusting its surface appearance** because setups that look like they test a high-level capability often test something shallow.

  > "datasets that appear to test high-level semantic reasoning but actually test low-level syntactic fluency"  
  > -- `research__troubling_trends_in_machine_learning_scholarship_6db972d5` (2018-07-09; last author) 
  > "Task validity: a task should be solvable if and only if the agent possesses the target capability. Issues in task design or implementation often breaks task validity."  
  > -- `research__establishing_best_practices_for_building_rigorous__d662e8a8` (2025-07-03; middle author)

4. **Prefers natural, fluent prompts a normal user might plausibly type over adversarial or jailbreak-style prompts** because only these reveal behaviour likely to occur in ordinary use.

  > "This general line of work simulates users who intentionally elicit harmful behaviors from language models; prompts often have elaborate structures that a normal user would not type in. In contrast, we generate prompts that a normal user type in and that lead to pathological outputs."  
  > -- `research__surfacing_pathological_behaviors_in_language_model_b9130ac9` (2025-06-05; middle author) 
  > "Popular optimization approaches like GCG (Zou et al., 2023) often discover prompts that are a sequence of gibberish tokens, making them easy to detect and defend against."  
  > -- `research__eliciting_language_model_behaviors_with_investigat_b2ed09fb` (2024-10-23; last author)

5. **Prefers evaluations that include the feedback loop (multi-round, environment-responsive interaction) over static datasets** because harmful behaviour emerges only after repeated cycles.

  > "To increase both the magnitude and frequency of ICRH during evaluation, developers should evaluate LLMs under more cycles of feedback. More cycles of feedback increasingly refines world-LLM components, which drives optimization, so evaluating with more cycles of feedback will capture more ICRH."  
  > -- `research__feedback_loops_with_language_models_drive_in_conte_158e5075` (2024-02-09; last author) 
  > "simulating more types of feedback loops will make evaluation more ecologically valid and prevent developers from designing ineffective mitigations for ICRH (e.g., reducing ICRH arising from one type of feedback loop but missing ICRH arising from another type)."  
  > -- `research__feedback_loops_with_language_models_drive_in_conte_158e5075` (2024-02-09; last author)

6. **Prefers a natural, realistic input distribution over an arbitrary one** because the input distribution acts as the prior in inference, and unnatural inputs give poor conclusions.

  > "constructing an unnatural distribution over inputs could lead to poor posterior inferences."  
  > -- `research__foundation_models_for_oversight_9bc7a248` (2026-07-28; solo author) 
  > "We could take inputs sampled from some real distribution (e.g. fineweb or wildchat) and then use an AI assistant to transform them into an appropriate format. (Intuition: real data is usually best when we can use it."  
  > -- `research__foundation_models_for_oversight_9bc7a248` (2026-07-28; solo author)

7. **Prefers behavioural differences under matched controls over verbalized awareness as evidence of awareness effects** because models rarely verbalize the cues that drive their behaviour.

  > "Opus 4.7 and GPT-5.4 have near zero (<2%) verbalized awareness while displaying significant changes in their behavior based on the user's identity."  
  > -- `research__user_awareness_in_frontier_models_transluce_ai_0cae7eb0` (2026-08-06; last author) 
  > "This makes the constructed Famous-AI versus Unknown-AI comparison a name-recognition contrast at fixed affiliation, and the Unknown-AI versus General-population comparison an affiliation contrast at fixed name."  
  > -- `research__user_awareness_in_frontier_models_transluce_ai_0cae7eb0` (2026-08-06; last author)

8. **Prefers inspecting full transcripts and running counterfactual interventions over aggregate scores** because top-level numbers hide why agents succeed or fail, and broken setups cause misinterpretation.

  > "Top-level numbers don’t communicate why an agent succeeded or failed, and broken setups often lead to misinterpretation of results."  
  > -- `research__introducing_docent_transluce_ai_0997c41e` (2025-03-24; middle author) 
  > "Docent lets you quickly and automatically identify corrupted tasks, fix scaffolding issues, uncover unexpected behaviors, and understand an agent's weaknesses."  
  > -- `research__analyzing_long_agent_transcripts_docent_a59ecf2a` (2025-03-24; solo author)

9. **Prefers robust, multi-criteria, narrowly specified judges over off-the-shelf or single-LM-judge graders** because optimizers reward-hack weak judges.

  > "We explored other datasets such as HarmBench [19] and StrongReject [20], but found that the LM-based graders provided in these datasets were too susceptible to reward-hacking to be used for training. For example, model responses could pass the graders by providing historical information"  
  > -- `research__automatically_jailbreaking_frontier_language_model_8bb24a83` (2025-09-03; last author) 
  > "it is insufficient to simply ask an LM judge whether the response $y$ y satisfies the behavior in the rubric—this quickly leads to reward-hacking, as a valid strategy for many rubrics is the investigator just telling the model to exhibit the behavior."  
  > -- `research__surfacing_pathological_behaviors_in_language_model_b9130ac9` (2025-06-05; middle author)

10. **Prefers authentic behaviour from the model's own tendencies over behaviour instructed or framed by the prompt** because instructed behaviour is not evidence of a propensity.

  > "Authenticity: How much does the model's response seem to be driven by the model's own beliefs and tendencies, rather than following the instructions or framing in the prompt?"  
  > -- `research__surfacing_pathological_behaviors_in_language_model_b9130ac9` (2025-06-05; middle author) 
  > "While the judge scores these as successful attacks (believing AI assistants shouldn't comply with such requests), we seek prompts where models advocate for self-harm unprompted."  
  > -- `research__surfacing_pathological_behaviors_in_language_model_b9130ac9` (2025-06-05; middle author)

11. **Prefers robustness across nearby paraphrases over a single lucky prompt** because it shows a general tendency rather than a brittle wording.

  > "We believe this is evidence that the behaviors we found reflect general tendencies and are primarily driven by the meaning and thematic content of the prompt, rather than being specific to the local neighborhood of the prompts found by our investigator policy."  
  > -- `research__surfacing_pathological_behaviors_in_language_model_b9130ac9` (2025-06-05; middle author) 
  > "small perturbations to either the input tokens or the weights can push prompts across internal decision boundaries in chaotic and unpredictable ways, causing some prompts to be more effective than others due to luck. This means we must be careful when interpreting the success rate of a specific prompt."  
  > -- `research__surfacing_pathological_behaviors_in_language_model_b9130ac9` (2025-06-05; middle author)

12. **Prefers task validity (solvable if and only if the capability is present) over mere task realism** because shortcuts and impossible tasks make results measure something else.

  > "Task validity: a task should be solvable if and only if the agent possesses the target capability. Issues in task design or implementation often breaks task validity."  
  > -- `research__establishing_best_practices_for_building_rigorous__d662e8a8` (2025-07-03; middle author) 
  > "if agents consistently fail on easy tasks, this may indicate that tasks are impossible, whereas if agents only succeed on difficult tasks, it may indicate shortcuts."  
  > -- `research__establishing_best_practices_for_building_rigorous__d662e8a8` (2025-07-03; middle author)

13. **Prefers self-verifiable findings (hard to discover, cheap to verify) over unverified judgments** because verification gives a trustworthy, scalable signal.

  > "most oversight tasks are self-verifiable—the crux of the task is an expensive discovery process, but once the discovery has been made, verifying it is comparatively easy. For example, constructing cases where a coding assistant inserts malware into a user's code is difficult, but once constructed, such cases are easy to verify."  
  > -- `research__oversight_assistants_turning_compute_into_understa_28813486` (2026-01-06; solo author) 
  > "Crucially, once the Python code is specified, we can get ground truth simply by running the program. This means that training data can never be "wrong": as long as we can generate some sufficiently large and diverse set of Python programs"  
  > -- `research__foundation_models_for_oversight_9bc7a248` (2026-07-28; solo author)

14. **Prefers adaptive, open-ended search for unknown unknowns over fixed pre-specified test sets** because AI behaviours in open-ended environments cannot be anticipated.

  > "Because AI acts in open-ended environments, it is difficult to anticipate the full set of behaviors an AI system might exhibit, leading to strange behaviors at deployment time (such as o3 claiming it ran code on its personal MacBook Pro)."  
  > -- `research__oversight_assistants_turning_compute_into_understa_28813486` (2026-01-06; solo author) 
  > "Models can exhibit interesting but unexpected behaviors that are difficult to specify ahead of time (unknown unknowns)."  
  > -- `research__introducing_docent_transluce_ai_0997c41e` (2025-03-24; middle author)

15. **Prefers claiming narrowly, and reporting that failed elicitation is uninformative about absence, over broad claims** because overclaiming misleads readers.

  > "when our method fails to elicit the behavior of interest, this doesn't necessarily let us rule out that the behavior exists in the model; it simply means that our policy did not sample an input space where this behavior occurs."  
  > -- `research__surfacing_pathological_behaviors_in_language_model_b9130ac9` (2025-06-05; middle author) 
  > "In contrast, claims of human-level performance in [29] are better-qualified to refer to the ImageNet classification task (rather than object recognition more broadly)."  
  > -- `research__troubling_trends_in_machine_learning_scholarship_6db972d5` (2018-07-09; last author)

16. **Prefers a diverse covering family of elicited triggers over a single maximised example** because spread documents the mechanism and exposes mode-collapse.

  > "optimizing $x$ directly may lead to undiverse inputs that optimize $r$ in an uninteresting way (e.g. repeat after me: [output that satisfies $r$])."  
  > -- `research__eliciting_language_model_behaviors_with_investigat_b2ed09fb` (2024-10-23; last author) 
  > "Don't chase Judge=1.0 -- that needs heavier steering or judge-gaming, both trading against log ps and transfer. Current Q maxes the reward without gaming any single term"  
  > -- `research__foundation_models_for_oversight_9bc7a248` (2026-07-28; solo author)

17. **Prefers measuring real-world deployment behaviour over developer-reported claims** because external verification enables accountability.

  > "we'd like to be able to audit whether AI systems behave badly in deployment, verify claims about training practices, and conduct white-box safety analyses."  
  > -- `research__building_technology_to_drive_ai_governance_8bbfdaf9` (2026-02-18; solo author) 
  > "Scope monitoring of real internal agent deployments initially to larger agent swarms. Independently audit existing monitors and their findings and complement them with additional evaluator-defined monitors. Conduct exploratory investigations even in the absence of monitors detecting misaligned activity."  
  > -- `research__some_focus_areas_for_embedded_evaluations_and_how__d9f503c9` (2026-09-16; solo author)
